children.name: By 2025, Malaysia has strengthened democratic governance, and all people living in Malaysia benefit from a more cohesive society, strengthened governance and participation.
children.description:
There has been an overall shift in Malaysia’s development planning focus from “macroeconomic resilience” to “more meaningful economic growth”34. A key tenet of this shift is embedded in governance reform through greater transparency and public-service efficiency35. A focus on good governance, accountability and transparency, at the institutional and individual level, and keeping social consciousness and environmental sustainability at the centre of economic growth have been identified as being critical to Malaysia escaping the “middle-income trap” and achieving its full potential, in line with the priorities of SDG 16, including peace/social cohesion, governance and human rights. The MTR of the Eleventh Plan lays out a holistic and high-impact agenda for governance reforms, reflecting the broad need for greater separation of powers across the executive, legislature and judiciary, strengthening checks and balances, and other specific aspects, including electoral reforms, strengthening anticorruption efforts, etc. The SPV 2030 also reinforces these reforms as continuing priorities.

One of the hallmarks of a democratic nation can be seen in the degree of independence, transparency and inclusivity of its institutions, as noted in the MTR of the Eleventh Plan’s agenda for governance reforms, and the inclusivity of its political processes — processes which, in essence, determine and reflect the ultimate will and representation of the people. These processes are seen in electoral institutions that are inclusive and responsive to the population, political parties that reflect the spectrum of values and ideologies of the society, and legislative bodies that are truly representative. The “Sustaining Peace and Good Governance Goal” (SDG 16) has specific significance for parliamentarians. SDG 16 aims to “promote peaceful and inclusive societies, providing access to justice for all and building effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels”, with targets 16.6 and 16.7 directly fitting with parliamentarian roles. Another important element is space for civil society, dissenting voices and freedom of media, which has regained ground in recent times, to be further consolidated and professionalised. In this regard, the Ministry of Home Affairs is in the process of amending the Printing Presses and Publications Act 1984. Malaysia’s legal framework should provide increased protection against discrimination, abuse, stigmatisation and harassment on the basis of age, gender, race, disability or other characteristics, and this protection should be effectively enforced.

The focus on greater accountability in the governance pillar of the MTR of the Eleventh Plan also means expanding public participation in policymaking, ensuring that development plans are inclusive, and taking into account local contexts and constituency-specific realities. Therefore, any significant reform of governance policies must necessarily touch on challenging issues, emphasising the need for inclusive engagement with stakeholders. The role of civil society in governance reform is vital in terms of it playing a constructive role in policy debates on reform, thereby ensuring inclusion as well as making civil society a partner in monitoring governance performance and in delivering public services to specific target communities.

The current state of federal-state-local government relations is also key. There is a need for increased policy coherence and implementation coordination across levels of government in order to enhance the effectiveness of development results in Malaysia. Thus, a clearer understanding of the linkages between processes and stronger and more extensive engagement at subnational levels are entry points for intervention.

Also important is the fact that, although Malaysia’s various plans and policies have articulated variations on the themes of social stability, social integration and social cohesion, the overall scope remains quite limited. In line with the MTR of the Eleventh Plan, a National Unity Advisory Council has been formed and emphasis has been placed on a needs-based approach and, with the SPV 2030, on equitable outcomes. In March 2020, a new Ministry of National Unity was formed to take this important agenda forward. Consistent engagement at all levels (policy, institutional and community) is required to holistically address these issues and ensure inclusion.

The COVID-19 crisis has disproportionately impacted poor and vulnerable groups. Malaysia recorded a spike in gender-based violence (GBV), and the lack of routine data collection and inclusion of GBV in national surveys hampers efforts to mitigate its prevalence in an effective manner. The pandemic has further deepened the issues faced by undocumented persons, migrants, refugees and asylum seekers – in relation to legal access to services and squalid living conditions that have put them at greater risk of infection.

Finally, it is essential to note that the inclusion and participation of women, youth and children remains a major challenge. This is evidenced by the low political participation of women (as measured by their active engagement and parity in leadership positions or in the legislature). For instance, while women make up almost 60 per cent of the civil service (excluding the police and the military), the 14th General Elections of 2018 and the current Government brought about only five women ministers and four deputy ministers (12.9 per cent); 14.4 per cent of seats in the lower house of Parliament, and only 19.4 per cent of seats in the upper house36. In the corporate sector, women only hold 15.7 per cent of board seats in publicly-listed companies (against a target of 30 per cent)37. Youth under 3038 also constitute a significant proportion of Malaysia’s population, and, with the recent lowering of the voting age to 18, youth will form a significant proportion of the electorate in the future. Currently, there are inadequate opportunities for the engagement and participation of adolescents in national and subnational decision-making processes that affect their well-being, as well as in political processes. Responding to these challenges will be key to: ensuring that the potential of Malaysia’s youthful human capital is maximised; building a cohesive, inclusive and caring society; and developing values and gender and social norms to allow young people to feel that they have a stake in the nation’s development, and that they have the power and opportunity to contribute to decision-making that affects them. Hence, additional targeted interventions aimed at youth participation are needed, especially in decision making, productive work, social cohesion and political processes.

projects.name: Refugee resettlement
projects.description: In close coordination with UNHCR, the Malaysian Government and the governments of receiving countries, IOM facilitates safe and orderly resettlement of vulnerable refugees and asylum seekers to third countries. As a result of these initiatives, the most vulnerable individuals including those with significant medical conditions from over 20 nationalities were able to start new lives in more than 10 host countries, where they have access to healthcare, employment, formal education, and pathways to citizenship. In CY 2022 IOM facilitated the resettlement of 4,367 refugees including medical screening, vaccinations and treatment for communicable diseases, and cultural orientation prior to departure to a new country. Resettlement and complimentary pathways are a vital protection tool to provide international protection and meet the specific needs of refugees in which life, liberty, safety, health or fundamental human rights are secured.

projects.name: Green and Resilient Recovery Local Action Grant
projects.description: In attaining the 2030 Agenda, it is important to consider that any transformation to the way communities live, and work must consider any social aspects in ensuring the delivery of equitable outcomes and sustainable livelihoods, especially for the disadvantaged communities, such as rural communities. Therefore, it is vital that any transformation is a Just Transition, to ensure that effort to "green" the economy are fair and inclusive. Just Transitions have become increasingly central to reaching the 2030 Agenda and in particular, climate change goals. As such, UNDP is attempting to create a local development model for just transitions in rural areas that combines aspects of renewable energy deployment, livelihood improvement through rural enterprises, and capacity building. Undertaken through a multi-stakeholder partnerships model, this project aims to support rural communities transition towards low-carbon energy solutions, produce green products that help boost incomes while reducing impact to environment, and enhance the market competitiveness of rural enterprises. Additionally, the approach undertaken by this project focuses on driving gender equality and empowerment to resolve the gender gap in entrepreneurship between men and women by focusing on increasing digital literacy skills and using e-commerce as a platform to boost incomes for women entrepreneurs. This project will be undertaken through a grant modality for suitable proposals to be undertaken on-the-ground in several locations across Malaysia.

projects.name: Unwaste: tackling waste trafficking to support a circular economy in South East Asia.
projects.description:
Implemented by UNODC in cooperation with UNEP and UNITAR, aims to fight trafficking in waste between the EU and Southeast Asia. It does so by promoting enhanced EU-ASEAN Member States partnerships, in support of ongoing efforts towards a circular economy transition, in line with the relevant policy frameworks, with four priority countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam. 
UNEP is responsible for the legal components, examining the legal framework in the ASEAN region on waste trafficking and a legal comparative analysis of the four priority countries. UNEP will also develop a policy paper on ‘obstacles waste trafficking poses to the develop of circular economy and best practices from EU and Asia’, and a mapping of existing multilateral mechanisms in place in Southeast Asia to prevent waste trafficking in support of the objectives of the Unwaste project.

projects.name: UN Joint Team on HIV and AIDS in Malaysia
projects.description:
The Joint Team rendered substantial support to the Malaysian Government in ensuring sustainable funding, advancing prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV services and expanding HIV services to hard-to-reach communities. Technical support to the Malaysian Country Coordinating Mechanism and the Malaysian AIDS Council led to a successful Global Fund for HIV grant proposal for the 2022-2025 period. Focused on the establishment of resilient and sustainable systems for health (RSSH) and the expansion of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) as a method of HIV prevention, the application secured US$ 1.5 million for the procurement of PrEP for 18 primary care clinics across Malaysia until December 2024. More than US$ 1 million was also allocated to strengthen community-led programmes, the national health management information system, and monitoring and evaluation for RSSH (WHO).

Malaysia achieved all the process and outcome indicator targets set in the Elimination of Mother-to-child Transmission of HIV (EMTCT) and Syphilis plan for the 2017-2020 period. In 2022, the Joint Team provided extensive technical support for the development and submission of the EMTCT maintenance report and worked closely with the Regional and Global Validation Secretariat and the Ministry of Health to address concerns including human rights, gender equality and community engagement, which were raised by Global Validation Advisory Committee (GVAC) during its 2021 virtual mission (WHO).

The newly launched Reaching the Unreached (RTU) agenda helped to identify key cross-cutting issues affecting marginalized populations, including the high prevalence of communicable diseases such as tuberculosis in East Malaysia and in prisons and other closed settings through a collaboration with relevant stakeholders (WHO). Intense advocacy and technical support to the Ministry of Health also resulted in the Government recognizing the need to strengthen laboratory capacity by expanding point-of-care testing systems in high-burden areas to eliminate logistical barriers and improve access to healthcare services (WHO).

To expand access to HIV services among key and vulnerable populations, 138 refugees and asylum seekers living with HIV accessed antiretroviral treatment with support from the Joint Team. Nongovernmental organizations also received support in providing treatment adherence support services for 172 persons living with HIV enrolled on treatment, rehabilitative and nursing care for 12 extremely vulnerable refugees as well as sexual and reproductive health, gender-based violence and HIV information and counselling services for 935 hard-to-reach women and girls and their spouses through regular mobile outreach programmes in the Northern region of the Peninsular Malaysia. Additionally, 128 pregnant women and girls received antenatal care while 270 were given regular access to contraceptives through the mobile programmes (UNHCR).

Technical assistance was provided to the National Anti-drugs Agency of Malaysia on the transition towards voluntary-community based treatment and care of people who use drugs, as well as on “Strong Families” family-skills substance use prevention among children and adolescents. The Malaysian Prisons Department also benefitted from technical support on the delivery of comprehensive packages of HIV services for people in prisons (UNODC).

projects.name: SEA circular project - solving plastic pollution at source in the South East Asia region
projects.description:
SEA circular project aims to reduce adverse impact of land-based plastic leakage into the marine environment by ensuring that less plastic is wasted at source and the management of the plastic value chain is improved in South-East Asia. Considering waste management systems in the region remain inadequate to process increasing amounts of plastic waste, the project focuses on the lifecycle stages of (i) Production of plastic products, (ii) Plastic use, and (iii) Collection / sorting / recycling to ensure that less plastic is wasted and strategically prevent plastic litter entering the ocean. 

Technical assistance for Malaysia: The Government has launched the National Policy and Action Plan on Marine Litter 2021-2030 and Roadmap towards Zero Single-Use Plastics 2018-2030, supported the implementation of the National Action Plan on Marine Litter and strengthen a national monitoring programme through a training on marine litter monitoring and assessment and baseline surveys. SEA circular also conducted a plastic waste perception survey among Malaysian consumers and businesses to inform the implementation of market-based solutions and behaviour change interventions towards less plastic wasted. 

Two pilot demonstrations were implemented in Malaysia (Petaling Jaya and Penang) in 2021, showing how cross-sectoral partnerships and collaborations can help city councils and municipalities promote innovative circular economy approaches and transformational changes to provide better integrated waste management solutions for the residents. 

A short film on– PLASTIK – was produced in Malaysia and launched on the World Environment Day 2022. 

In the extension phase of the project 2023 -2024, the project will focus on regional guidance on Extended Producer Responsibility ( EPR) and Resuse Schemes

projects.name: Climate Finance Network
projects.description: Asia and Pacific countries are amongst the most vulnerable to climate change. The impacts of climate change are increasingly disrupting national economies and affecting livelihoods, water, energy, transportation, agriculture and ecosystems at an unprecedented scale. It is usually the poorest and the most vulnerable who are most at risk of the storms, floods, droughts, wildfires and rising sea levels, while lacking protections and resources to adapt. At the same time, here is growing recognition that affordable, scalable solutions are possible both for mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions and adaptation – and that these solutions can enable all of us to leapfrog to cleaner, more resilient economies. However, these call for policy and financing shifts away from business as usual to actively factor in climate change as well as ensure co-benefits and a focus on the needs of the most vulnerable. Over the past five years there has been an increase in the interest and capacity of Ministries of Finance, who are the main programme counterparts, to respond to climate change as well as take more integrated approaches to addressing and financing the social, environmental and economic objectives of the 2030 Agenda and take forward commitments under the Paris Agreement. This area of work is likely to acquire even further importance in light of the Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) of the IPCC and the momentum that has built on the in the wake of COVID-19 to recover forward better. The DFID-supported Climate Proofing Growth and Development (CPGD) programme (2013-2019) and the Government of Sweden supported Strengthening the Governance of Climate Change Finance to Enhance Gender Equality (GCCF) programmes (2017-22; previous phase 2012-16) have hitherto sought to respond to this demand by providing technical support for policy and technical policy reforms and interventions across the budget cycle ; as well as supporting the a promotion of sharing of knowledge and innovative ways to tap into expertise and offer peer-to-peer technical assistance across the region. Based on the success of the CPGD and GCCF programmes, a Climate Finance Network (CFN) is being proposed. It will serve as a peer-to-peer network and as a knowledge management and technical support facility to support Ministries of Finance with the engagement of sector ministries and sub-national governments to identify and scale up climate finance innovations in the region. In collaboration with stakeholders and partners the CFN will harness the momentum in climate finance reforms in ways that will allow knowledge to be shared in real-time across countries to facilitate acceleration and adoption/replication of climate budget planning and finance across governments as well as mobilization of public, private and blended climate finance. The CFN will work across on six inter-related workstreams which are based on our climate change finance programming experience over the past five years and lessons learnt during the inception phase of the CFN: 1) Climate change aligned budgeting and planning; 2) Direct access to international climate change finance; 3) Tax and use of innovative climate change financing instruments; 4) Gender and social inclusion and climate change finance; and 5) Transparency and accountability of climate change finance; and 6) Modelling climate change impacts on economic growth, sectors and consideration of distributional impacts

The Joint Team rendered substantial support to the Malaysian Government in ensuring sustainable funding, advancing prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV services and expanding HIV services to hard-to-reach communities. Technical support to the Malaysian Country Coordinating Mechanism and the Malaysian AIDS Council led to a successful Global Fund for HIV grant proposal for the 2022-2025 period. Focused on the establishment of resilient and sustainable systems for health (RSSH) and the expansion of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) as a method of HIV prevention, the application secured US$ 1.5 million for the procurement of PrEP for 18 primary care clinics across Malaysia until December 2024. More than US$ 1 million was also allocated to strengthen community-led programmes, the national health management information system, and monitoring and evaluation for RSSH (WHO).

Malaysia achieved all the process and outcome indicator targets set in the Elimination of Mother-to-child Transmission of HIV (EMTCT) and Syphilis plan for the 2017-2020 period. In 2022, the Joint Team provided extensive technical support for the development and submission of the EMTCT maintenance report and worked closely with the Regional and Global Validation Secretariat and the Ministry of Health to address concerns including human rights, gender equality and community engagement, which were raised by Global Validation Advisory Committee (GVAC) during its 2021 virtual mission (WHO).

The newly launched Reaching the Unreached (RTU) agenda helped to identify key cross-cutting issues affecting marginalized populations, including the high prevalence of communicable diseases such as tuberculosis in East Malaysia and in prisons and other closed settings through a collaboration with relevant stakeholders (WHO). Intense advocacy and technical support to the Ministry of Health also resulted in the Government recognizing the need to strengthen laboratory capacity by expanding point-of-care testing systems in high-burden areas to eliminate logistical barriers and improve access to healthcare services (WHO).

To expand access to HIV services among key and vulnerable populations, 138 refugees and asylum seekers living with HIV accessed antiretroviral treatment with support from the Joint Team. projects.name: UN Joint Team on HIV and AIDS in Malaysia
projects.description:
The Joint Team rendered substantial support to the Malaysian Government in ensuring sustainable funding, advancing prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV services and expanding HIV services to hard-to-reach communities. Technical support to the Malaysian Country Coordinating Mechanism and the Malaysian AIDS Council led to a successful Global Fund for HIV grant proposal for the 2022-2025 period. Focused on the establishment of resilient and sustainable systems for health (RSSH) and the expansion of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) as a method of HIV prevention, the application secured US$ 1.5 million for the procurement of PrEP for 18 primary care clinics across Malaysia until December 2024. More than US$ 1 million was also allocated to strengthen community-led programmes, the national health management information system, and monitoring and evaluation for RSSH (WHO).

Malaysia achieved all the process and outcome indicator targets set in the Elimination of Mother-to-child Transmission of HIV (EMTCT) and Syphilis plan for the 2017-2020 period. In 2022, the Joint Team provided extensive technical support for the development and submission of the EMTCT maintenance report and worked closely with the Regional and Global Validation Secretariat and the Ministry of Health to address concerns including human rights, gender equality and community engagement, which were raised by Global Validation Advisory Committee (GVAC) during its 2021 virtual mission (WHO).

The newly launched Reaching the Unreached (RTU) agenda helped to identify key cross-cutting issues affecting marginalized populations, including the high prevalence of communicable diseases such as tuberculosis in East Malaysia and in prisons and other closed settings through a collaboration with relevant stakeholders (WHO). Intense advocacy and technical support to the Ministry of Health also resulted in the Government recognizing the need to strengthen laboratory capacity by expanding point-of-care testing systems in high-burden areas to eliminate logistical barriers and improve access to healthcare services (WHO).

To expand access to HIV services among key and vulnerable populations, 138 refugees and asylum seekers living with HIV accessed antiretroviral treatment with support from the Joint Team. Nongovernmental organizations also received support in providing treatment adherence support services for 172 persons living with HIV enrolled on treatment, rehabilitative and nursing care for 12 extremely vulnerable refugees as well as sexual and reproductive health, gender-based violence and HIV information and counselling services for 935 hard-to-reach women and girls and their spouses through regular mobile outreach programmes in the Northern region of the Peninsular Malaysia. Additionally, 128 pregnant women and girls received antenatal care while 270 were given regular access to contraceptives through the mobile programmes (UNHCR).

Technical assistance was provided to the National Anti-drugs Agency of Malaysia on the transition towards voluntary-community based treatment and care of people who use drugs, as well as on “Strong Families” family-skills substance use prevention among children and adolescents. The Malaysian Prisons Department also benefitted from technical support on the delivery of comprehensive packages of HIV services for people in prisons (UNODC).

projects.name: Understanding Pathways to Adolescent Pregnancy in Southeast Asia
projects.description:
This study, conducted in Malaysia as part of a wider Southeast Asia study, is a collaboration between the Burnet Institute, UNFPA, and UNICEF. The study aims to improve understanding of the drivers and pathways to adolescent pregnancy in Southeast Asia and inform effective policy and programming responses. The primary objective of the study is to identify and explore the drivers and pathways to both intended and unintended adolescent pregnancy in Southeast Asia, including the relationship with early marriage/union. The study's secondary objective is to develop policy and programming recommendations, co-created with adolescents, to effectively address adolescent pregnancy.

The report was launched on 18 October 2023 as a joint initiative by UNFPA Malaysia and UNICEF Malaysia and was developed by the Burnet Institute.  The report included in-depth interviews with 45 adolescent girls from three states in Malaysia – Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, and Pahang, and highlighted six pathways to adolescent pregnancy. The reports underscore the importance of adolescent-responsive health services, comprehensive sexuality education, supportive relationships, and enabling environments that empower girls to make informed decisions about their sexual and reproductive health and lives.

projects.name: Qualitative assessment on sexual and reproductive health and rights, and health service access among women living with HIV in Malaysia.
projects.description: Malaysia received the certification for successful validation of elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV and syphilis in October 2018 making it the first country in the WHO Western Pacific Region to achieve such status and the second country in the Asia and the Pacific region after Thailand. Upon the validation, the Global Validation Advisory Committee has made the recommendations that include Malaysia to conduct a national study of stigma and discrimination faced by people living with HIV by supporting networks and associations of people living with HIV. Against this background a qualitative assessment on sexual and reproductive health and rights and access to healthcare services among women living with HIV was conducted in collaboration with women living with HIV community, NGOs working for people living with HIV and key populations and Malaysian AIDS Council. The assessment was led by a research team from Universiti Sains Malaysia with technical and coordination support from a regional multistakeholder advisory committee that oversees and provides strategic direction for the key steps of the research process. UNAIDS contributed both technical and financial support to sexual and reproductive health and rights assessment and the findings of the assessment were fed into the maintenance review of Malaysia’s validation of elimination of mother-to-child transmission. The findings of the qualitative assessment reflect the views and experiences of many of the women living with HIV in Malaysia.

projects.name: Sabah Report Launch: Demographic and Socioeconomic Changes in Sabah
projects.description:
The Sabah Report Launch, a collaborative effort between the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Malaysia Country Office, the University Malaysia Sabah (UMS), and the University of Malaya (UM), provided a comprehensive overview of demographic shifts and socioeconomic changes in Sabah. The Sabah Report Launch presented a comprehensive overview of Sabah's demographic shifts and socioeconomic changes, emphasising the significance of investing in women and youth for sustainable development. The report, a collaborative effort between the University of Malaya (UM), University Malaysia Sabah (UMS), and UNFPA, serves as a critical tool for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing tangible benchmarks for gender equity in Sabah. The report's findings underscored the necessity of addressing issues like internal migration, income differentials, and the impact on women, youth, and non-citizens in Sabah.

The report unveiled critical demographic dynamics, indicating a rapid population rise driven by foreign workers. Sabah, with a fertility rate of 1.4, faces challenges related to an ageing population and gender inequality impacting national development. The book addressed the importance of policies enabling men to share parental responsibilities and reducing barriers keeping women from the workforce. Critical issues such as child marriage, education, and literacy skills affecting women's socioeconomic status were highlighted, emphasising the need for collaboration with various entities to address these challenges. The gender narrative stressed the importance of increasing female productivity and labour force participation. Initiatives such as parental leave policies and the need for social and behavioural change to encourage shared responsibilities were discussed. Challenges related to family planning, healthcare access, and gender data gaps were addressed. The insights will guide future policies and strategies to foster sustainable development, particularly in empowering women and youth for a thriving Sabah.

projects.name: Building the Capacity of Health Staff in Behavioural Science
projects.description:
Behavioural sciences are increasingly used by governments, ministries of health and other public health agencies to gain an evidence-based understanding of how people behave and make decisions. This understanding can assist in designing and implementing interventions, programs, and policies to generate change in health behaviours in a sustainable, equitable, and efficient manner to deliver better health outcomes. This was recognised not only by WHO but also by the Member States at the 76th World Health Assembly (WHA) with the passing of the ‘Behavioural sciences for better health’ resolution.  

WHO Representative Office to Malaysia, Brunei Darussalam, and Singapore (WCO) is working with the Ministries of Health in Malaysia and Brunei Darussalam to strengthen capacities and implement projects using tools and methodologies from the behavioural sciences. To date, WCO and WHO BI Unit at HQ, in collaboration with the Ministries and other partners, have delivered trainings and workshops, provided technical and strategic guidance for the establishment of BI units/functions, and conducted joint projects and research. WHO assisted the Malaysian government with developing and sponsoring the global resolution. Recently WCO has employed a short-term behavioural and social sciences consultant to further support this work.    

The Ministry of Health Malaysia (MOH) established the Behavioural Insights Unit (BIU) within the Institute for Health Behavioural Research (IHBR) in 2022. Today, BIU partners with various MOH divisions responsible for policy and programs, in the application of the behavioural sciences and integration of a behavioural lens into program and policy design, and implementation. The value of behaviourally informed policies, projects and programs has been promoted across MOH and the demand for advice and technical assistance from the BIU has rapidly grown.    

MOH has requested capacity building training in the form of a 3-day physical workshop for approximately 30 participants. This concept note details the delivery of a TOT package to build sustainable BI capacity for BIU. The training would be based on the recently designed and tested package by WHO BI Unit at HQ.

- Communicate why behavioural science is important to public health, for individual behaviours, program and service delivery, and policy development.

- Identify the ethical dimensions and considerations of applying behavioural insights.  
- Deliver a BI introductory course to their organisational peers.

projects.name: Event-Based Surveillance Protocol for Laboratory Investigation
projects.description:
Proper detection of disease-causing organisms is very critical in controlling the course of outbreaks and avoiding large-scale epidemics. Traditionally, the laboratory response to an emerging event is influenced by the risk assessment done by the clinician or front liner. Thus, the testing would be specific based on the suspected agent etiology. However, based on the monitoring of outbreak samples received by the National Public Health Laboratory (NPHL) and Regional Public Health Laboratories (RPHLs) in 2018- 2022, the yield of detection rate is in the range of 17-60 % with an average of 32%. This demonstrates that most of the causative agents causing the outbreak remains unknown.  

To improve the performance of laboratory diagnostics, the knowledge gaps would need to be systemically identified which involves the whole process, from sampling strategy, samples management, samples processing, testing, and interpretation of test results. This will be more challenging when dealing with rare pathogens or novel pathogens. Therefore, this workshop is aimed to come up with a good model to improve laboratory diagnostic preparedness through the application of an event-based approach.  Using the event-based surveillance protocol, a risk assessment will be done based on etiological agents potentially causing the disease and the syndrome of clinical presentation. This protocol will guide good sampling techniques of clinical specimens as well as other related specimens including environment and food specimens during field investigation, and more importantly, laboratory investigation in response to any potential event of diseases including diseases due to novel pathogens.   

 35 participants were trained.

The objective of this activity is to develop a Manual on Event-Based Surveillance Protocol for Laboratory Investigation.  

Participants will be from MOH:   
Infectious diseases specialist and toxicologist 
Pathologist 
Public Health physician 
Family health medicine specialist 
Science officers/subject matter experts

projects.name: Strengthening Laboratory Capacity on environment samples: hands-on training and guidelines development from sample collection, processing, and pathogen detection for Public Health Laboratories
projects.description:
Strengthening Laboratory Capacity on environment samples: hands-on training and guidelines development from sample collection, processing, and pathogen detection for Public Health Laboratories. 

The National Public Health Laboratory (NPHL), Ministry of Health (MOH), Malaysia, plays a vital role as a key laboratory at the national level for public health. It is responsible for providing essential support services for outbreak management and implementing control measures for public health concerns, for both clinical and environmental samples. The environmental samples encompass sewerage water, soil, as well as water from lakes, rivers, swimming pools, and other sources.  

Environmental sample has been one of the fundamental tools to support epidemiology investigation and outbreak pertaining to pathogens relating to the environment that causes a potential threat to the human race. Water sampling in public health care settings is used to detect waterborne pathogens of clinical significance or to determine the quality of finished water in a community distribution system. Routine testing of the water is usually not indicated, but sampling and confirmed laboratory results in support of outbreak investigations can help determine preventive and control measures. It is also essential to monitor for a potentially hazardous environmental condition, confirm the presence of hazardous chemical or biological agents, and validate the successful abatement of the hazard. 

To date, NPHL has detected pathogens such as viruses (SARs-CoV-2, Poliovirus, Rotavirus and Enterovirus) and bacteria’s (Leptospira spp, Legionella spp and Burkholderia pseudomallei) from environmental samples.  

In the past few years, Malaysia had faced few outbreaks and increased in mortality which has raised concern to public health. For example: 
Leptospira outbreak in National Training Service Centre @ PLKN in 2012. Water activity (rivers or pools) is no-longer part of training centre activities. 
Legionella outbreak at shopping centre, KL business centre, in 2013 
Rotavirus outbreak at Batang Padang and Hilir Perak District, Perak in 2012 
Poliovirus outbreak in Sabah in year 2019 
Pandemic SARS-Cov-2 from year 2020-2023  

Currently, we are employing the ultrafiltration method to collect samples. However, the pathogen detection results are proving to be very poor. Therefore, the primary objective of this project is to enhance the laboratory's capacity by providing training to the personnel from public health laboratorie (NPHL and four Public Health Laboratories) on various approaches and methodologies for environmental sample collection, processing, and pathogen detection via molecular approach. Additionally, we aim to develop guidelines for environmental sampling specifically tailored for pathogen detection. This endeavor will enable us to improve the accuracy and efficiency of pathogen detection in environmental samples. 

12 participants were sent to Singapore for the training. 

General Objective 
To train public health laboratories on environmental sampling, samples processing and testing including develop guidelines for the identification of pathogens (novel, emerging and re-emerging) from environmental samples. 

Specific Objectives 
To develop the capacity and capability for the most reliable sampling collection method for the detection of environmental pathogens. 
To develop environmental sampling guidelines to be used as national reference. 
To perform environmental sampling at the ground level with the verified techniques. 
To determine the correct environmental sample handling (includes collection, packaging and transportation).  
To perform samples processing and pathogens detection including Next Gene Sequencing (NGS) from environmental samples. (This consist of 2 sessions – labelled as 5a & 5b under proposed timeline) 
To establish the molecular epidemiologically linkages from the environmental pathogens to clinical samples in disease outbreaks.

projects.name: Implementation of a pharmacy-based HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) service delivery model to increase PrEP uptake in Malaysia
projects.description:
Implementation of a pharmacy-based HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) service delivery model to increase PrEP uptake in Malaysia

Since 2010, the overall trend of new HIV infections in Malaysia has plateaued, with only a modest 0.9% decline. Several risk factors for HIV infection have been identified. For example, condom use was reported to be less than 80% among MSM and less than 30% among PWID. Engagement in chem sex is also on the rise among MSM, putting them at high risk of HIV as a result of inconsistent condom use, long hours of sexual activities, multiple sex partners, and group sex being reported.  

Despite being high-risk populations, MSM and FSW are reported to have low access to HIV prevention services. Currently, PrEP is only prescribed and dispensed in clinics and hospitals in both private and public settings. There are still no official statistics on the number of PrEP users in Malaysia. PrEPWatch estimates that the cumulative number of people initiating PrEP in Malaysia is 130 in 2022 but based on unofficial estimates, less than 2,500 people are taking PrEP. 

Exploring novel PrEP service delivery models outside of medical facilities such as pharmacy-based PrEP service delivery model is important to demedicalise and expand the reach of PrEP. This project will address the current knowledge gap and inform the viability of a pharmacy-based PrEP service delivery model as a novel PrEP implementation strategy in increasing PrEP uptake in Malaysia. This project will also provide valuable information to stakeholders in the Asia-Pacific region keen to explore this model for PrEP scale-up.  

16 community pharmacies were trained from this programme.

projects.name: Strengthening Laboratory Capacity on Viral Metagenomics (Human Sample) for Public Health Laboratories: A Hands-On Training
projects.description:
The field of virology has seen a rapid evolution, driven by the need to detect and understand emerging infectious diseases, particularly viral pathogens. The National Public Health Laboratory (NPHL) and the four regional Public Health Laboratories (PHLs) are the key laboratories in Malaysia that involves in disease surveillance, diagnosis, response on infectious diseases outbreaks under the Ministry of Health, Malaysia. Whereas the National Institutes of Health (NIH) operates as research body under the Ministry of Health Malaysia (MOH), while the Institute for Medical Research (IMR) falls under the purview of NIH. Both the NPHL and IMR serve as the respective National Influenza Lab (NIL) and the National Influenza Centre (NICs) in Malaysia. It is where surveillance samples are tested, and PCR subtyping is performed. During the COVID-19 pandemic, IMR was also involved in the diagnosis and genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2. 

Therefore, to equip these laboratories with the latest tools and techniques, there is a pressing need to strengthen laboratory capacity in viral genomic surveillance, with a specific focus on respiratory viruses such as the influenza virus (IFV) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). This aligns with the WHO Global Genomic Surveillance Strategy for Pathogens with Pandemic and Epidemic Potential, 2022–2032. 

This project proposal outlines a comprehensive hands-on training program designed to enhance the capabilities of public health laboratories and NIH in the field of viral genomic surveillance. The knowledge acquired from this training is valuable for developing laboratory sequencing capabilities in the NPHL, PHLs, and NIH in Malaysia. With new and emerging pathogens being discovered worldwide, it's crucial for PHLs and NIH to detect these pathogens. Maintaining continuity in viral genomic sequencing at PHLs and NIH will enable scientists and lab technicians to enhance their knowledge and skills, thereby increasing the likelihood of early detection of harmful and infectious pathogens. 

Project description 
- This project is a hands-on training workshop designed to strengthen viral genomic work and its applications in viral genomic surveillance capabilities among PHLs and NIH, Malaysia. 
- This training will focus the technical aspects including both wet lab and bioinformatics for laboratorians to perform viral genomic sequencing using ONT platform.  
- Components of project consists of: Lectures (theory) and Hands-on (Practical and training workshop) and troubleshooting 
- Importance of the hands-on component of the training programme is that the participants will go through the full workflow in the laboratory to become technically competent in viral genomic sequencing and bioinformatics analysis. 

General Objective 
- To train the member staff of public health laboratories and National Institute of Health, Malaysia on laboratory techniques required for viral genomic sequencing in order to identify novel, emerging and re-emerging pathogens. 

Specific Objective 
- To perform viral genomic sequencing using ONT Platform  
- To develop analysis skill in viral genomic sequences using readily available and user-friendly software. 
- To develop testing protocols for viral genomic sequencing using ONT Platform as well as bioinformatic analysis for genomic characterization and epidemiology 
- To learn primer design for whole genome sequencing
